c) Excerpts from the letters of Emilia Settimo, Princess of Fitalia, to Mother Rosa Gattorno (unpublished; AFSA G.4.33).

Excerpts from 10 letters are reproduced here (out of the 40 existing in all), from which a concrete and well-grounded demonstration emerges that Sister Anna del Salvatore was a woman particularly favored by divine grace.

Emilia di Fitalia, already an intimate friend and great admirer of the virtues of Sister Anna del Salvatore, having become, after the Servant of God's death, a spiritual daughter of Mother Rosa Gattorno, establishes with her a relationship of very great esteem and veneration, which leads her to share with her all her experiences and to ask her advice for her spiritual journey.

The reference to Sister Anna del Salvatore is constant, and deep is her sorrow over her untimely passing.

1. Letter of 7/27/1884 (AFSA G.4.33).

She agrees to the proposal to build a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Lourdes in the new church in Rome. She communicates the news of her own father's death; in her grief, the Superior, Sister Anna del Salvatore, whom she considers a true mother, has been a great comfort to her.

Most Reverend Mother,

Before leaving Palermo for a journey of several months, I wish to express to you my thanks for the proposal made to me of building a chapel in your church.

I feel very unworthy of such an honor, but very happy to be able to contribute to the glory of our Most Holy Mother under the title of Our Lady of Lourdes, to whom I would like to dedicate the chapel. [...]

An unexpected misfortune made me interrupt this letter for several days; the Lord has called to Himself my dearest Father, whom I hoped to see again soon.

It is a great consolation to me to take this occasion to commend his soul to your prayers, together with the hearts of his children, afflicted by such a loss.

I have no words to express how much comfort and support the Superior, Sister Anna Salvatore, who is a true mother to me, has given me. [...]

Accept, Most Reverend Mother, the expression of my most profound devotion, and bless me in the Lord.

Your

most affectionate daughter in J. C.

Emilia di Fitalia

Palermo 7/27/84

2. Letter of 4/11/1885 (AFSA G.4.33).

Sister Anna del Salvatore has returned to Palermo content, even though she suffered during the journey. She underscores how it is a blessing for the city of Palermo to have the presence of so great and dear a person.

Palermo, April 11, 1885

My dearest Mother,

[...] Our dear Superior worked wonders during her journey through Sicily, suffering all that one can suffer during a trip, and more besides. She was jolted for 12 hours in a horrible carriage, on a road covered with stones, she traveled on a tiny, terrible little steamboat during weather that was anything but calm; in short, she enjoyed every suffering, and returned most content. I imagine how displeased she would be if she knew I am giving you all these descriptions.

Ah! my dearest Mother, what a blessing for all of us to have in Palermo so great and dear a soul! [...]

Kissing your hand, my dearest Mother, I beg you to bless me together with my husband and my loved ones, and believe me forever

Your most affectionate daughter in J. C.

Emilia

3. Letter, undated, but likely of May 1885 (AFSA G.4.33).

She reports on the health of Sister Anna del Salvatore: although she is better, she is very weak and suffers with the serenity and joy of a saint. She regrets not being in a position to give the Mother her own news in person.

My dearest Mother,

[...]

Thanks to the Lord, Sister A[nna] Salvatore is doing better, but is still very weak and suffering. Not being very easy in my mind about her condition, I asked Dr. Cataliotti to come and see her, and after examining her yesterday he told us the Superior had miliary fever, but fortunately a very mild case. He prescribed her quinine if her fever was below 39, and antipyrine if above 39.

Our dear sick woman suffers with the patience and cheerfulness of a saint; the only thing that brings tears to her eyes is the thought that you, my dearest Mother, are distressed to know she is suffering, and that she cannot give you her own news in person. Yesterday, after I left her, she sent me two Sisters to ask me for Lourdes water, and this morning she had word sent to me that she is doing much better. I am certain that the Most Holy Virgin will make her well soon, and that we shall owe one more debt of gratitude to our heavenly Mother, so full of mercy towards us.

I believe that Sister A[nna] Salvatore's illness also has something supernatural about it, but the physical illness exists too, and the miliary fever can even be smelled. She has a great loss of appetite and takes nothing but a little clear jellied broth, which Maria Teresa sends her, and milk with iced egg yolks. She much enjoys taking, from time to time, a little piece of ice in her mouth.

It is truly laughable how many little things that ugly demon contrives to vex us all, and especially the most good Sister A[nna] Salvatore, but she accepts everything with such a cheerful patience that it gives strength to everyone.

If only I could stay night and day beside our dear sick woman, but the devil fears that these beautiful examples will do me too much good, and puts obstacles in my way at every step; to the point that today I must resign myself not to go, for the sake of peace, and must content myself with the news they send me. [...]

Bless me, my dearest Mother, and believe me forever

Your most affectionate daughter in J. C.

Emilia

4. Letter of 6/8/1885 (AFSA G.4.33).

Deeply grieved by the death of Sister Anna del Salvatore, she describes in great detail her last hours on this earth: her fortitude in suffering, her conscious joy at going to meet death, and the profound piety with which she received the viaticum and the anointing of the sick.

Palermo, June 8, 1885

Dearest Mother,

Immersed in the deepest grief, I find no other comfort, apart from prayer, than to write to you and share with you the anguish of your heart. Oh! how the Lord tests us by taking from us our dearest Sister A[nna del] Salvatore! It still seems to me to be in a horrible dream, and there are moments when I still cannot believe the cruel reality!

I imagine how grieved you must be, my most beloved Mother, knowing what tender affection bound you to your dear Sister A[nna] Salvatore. The Lord knows what He does, and despite the anguish of my heart, I try to resign myself to His Holy Will and say that fiat which the Superior uttered as she expired.

I cannot tell you, dearest Mother, how orphaned I feel without this blessed soul, who was the tenderest, sweetest Mother to me! In all my sorrows, in all my little vexations, in doubts, in uncertainties, I would run to her, and always found comfort, help, light and peace with her! I shall never be able to express all I owe her, and only the Lord can repay it for me, increasing to infinity her glory and blessedness.

When I last wrote to you, I was certain that within a very few days we would see her again, healed, full of life and activity, and despite the fact that her illness was worsening, no one believed that in so short a time we would lose her. I called another doctor, Dr. Cataliotti, who inspired great confidence in our dear departed one; he ordered a treatment, but even he did not believe her in danger. She, however, knew her end was near, and little by little prepared us, forgetting even herself until the very last. Twice I saw her weep, she, the strong woman of the Gospel, weeping she said "I cannot bear to think of the Mother's sorrow," and her heart broke at this thought.

On the morning of the 7th, the day of her death, she said to the Sisters, "what a beautiful day, what a happy day." As her illness worsened, Our Lord was exposed to give her the Holy Viaticum; you can imagine with what feelings she received it. Sister Macrina, with another Sister, came to tell me, and I ran at once, first telling Cataliotti to come as soon as possible. I found the dearest Superior calm and serene, but her face already bearing the shadows of death. I still did not want to believe the cruel truth, and asked her, being alone with her, "My Mother, is it true that you will recover soon?" She answered me, "It is unlikely that I can recover, but the Lord can do all things." Her thoughts always turned to you, dearest Mother, and she submitted to every remedy in order to recover and spare you this sorrow.

She asked me to have Sister Teresa pray with this intention; I wrote to her at once, as well as to the Capuchin Sisters, asking them to expose the Blessed Sacrament and beg the Lord to leave her to us! She let me see this desire, and added "you must not think that I am not resigned to die, but it is for the Mother's sake, I would like to make an act of obedience to the Mother."

She suffered greatly, but serenity never left her. I told her that everyone was praying for her recovery, but that she too must pray for it. At once she answered: "Yes, oh! my good Jesus, heal me so that I may obey the Mother"; these words she spoke in so sublime a manner that the Sisters and I could not hold back our tears. Often she repeated "The Lord wills it so" and "fiat," "fiat." She also said, with a burst of joy, "What a beautiful day! What a beautiful day!"

Towards midday Cataliotti came, found her much worse, gave her antipyrine and prescribed bile drinks because her stomach kept swelling more and more; for a week she had had no bowel movement, and no remedy helped. Once the doctor left, Maria Teresa and Sister Teresa came, and the dearest Superior was most pleased to see them. Sister Teresa remained alone with the sick woman for a while and proposed to anoint her with oil taken from the lamp of the Blessed Sacrament. After the anointing she gave her an enema with castor oil, and this relieved her a little. She repeated the anointing twice more and gave two more bile enemas, as the doctor had ordered. Her abdomen became a little softer, and the dearest Superior felt somewhat relieved, and our hearts began to open to hope.

Around 4:30, my husband came to fetch me for dinner, and Sister Teresa too prepared to leave. The Superior gave thanks for the smallest things, with her overflowing heart, and I had to leave her, not suspecting how little the improvement would last. In thought and with all the powers of my soul I was with her, but I could not return before seven in the evening.

As soon as I arrived, the Sisters told me she was worse; I went in a few minutes later and found her much more changed than in the morning; the fever burned her, and a rattle in her chest was beginning to make her breathing most distressing. She could utter only broken words; she often said "the Lord wills it so," or "fiat." For each of us she had a look of affection, a word of thanks, a sweet word. But the illness kept worsening, and Monsignor Zuccaro came in around 8 o'clock, he too proposing a remedy for her: the Holy Oil. The Superior said, "Yes, I am ready"; the candles were lit, and in the presence of the Sisters, of several priests, and of me, Fr. Filiti administered to her the Last Sacrament.

Her breathing grew ever more difficult, her sufferings increased, her extremities began to grow cold; mustard plasters were applied, but nothing, it did not help. Sister Battistina arrived shortly after to spend the night; she too had stayed a good part of the day and left promising to return in the evening, her presence being a relief to everyone. She supported the dear Superior, helping her in every way, but death drew ever nearer.

The Superior kept kissing her Crucifix, saying "My Jesus, mercy," or fiat, despite her difficulty in speaking. It was a picture of desolation to see her suffer so, and with such holy resignation that it would have moved stones. In the midst of her sufferings she smiled, looking at me, and I could not believe that we were to lose her.

I do not know whether it was only an impression of mine, but it seemed to me that I was seeing a victim offering herself up, and that the hand of the Lord was weighing more heavily upon his favorite creature, in order to be able to forgive guilty sinners, that is, me and so many others. Besides, the dear Superior had made me understand this several months before; we had been speaking of punishments, of cholera, and I asked her, "Mother, what do you think, shall we have the cholera?" She answered me, "Let us hope not; in that way a victim will be found to appease the Lord." These words made a great impression on me and brought me a strong fear that she was speaking of herself, but I drove it away, thinking: the Superior is at the head of a community, she knows how necessary she is to souls, it cannot be her, she must know of some other soul, and I calmed myself. And yet it was only too true!

Around 9:30 my husband came to fetch me; I begged him to let me stay for the night; he would not agree, but left me a little longer. The dearest dying woman continued to suffer; a restlessness seized her, she wanted to get out of bed, but we would not allow it, for fear she might die while rising. Despite this great desire of hers, she resigned herself to suffer in stillness, like Our Lord, and said "fiat, fiat."

The Sisters surrounded her, desolate; Sister A. Macrina did not trust herself to witness this painful scene, and I believe she was praying in the chapel. At 10 o'clock my husband came back for me, and I had to resign myself to leaving her who was more than a Mother to me! I knelt by her bed, kissed her hand, and asked her to bless me; she raised the hand that had so benefited me, sustained me and drawn me towards the good, made a cross on my forehead (as I had asked her to do almost every time I had seen her in the past) and stroked my cheek. I said to her, "then, my Mother, do you promise to always help me with your advice, with your prayers?" She answered, "Yes," looking at me. I rose, and not trusting myself to look at her, I left the room weeping. The Sisters told me afterwards that she waved to me twice more with her hand.

Three quarters of an hour later, at a quarter to eleven, she expired with the word fiat on her lips, her hands joined in prayer. She blessed all the Sisters, who kissed her hand one by one. To the Confessor's request that she leave a keepsake for her daughters, she said "let them be good." Sister Macrina also told me that she said "let them hold fast to their vocation, faithful to the rules." She looked at the Sisters one by one, and many felt as though she were reading each one's future.

The next day I saw her in her sublime peace; she seemed alive to us all, and we expected to hear from her smiling mouth some sweet word of comfort and hope. A photograph was taken for you, dearest Mother. The idea came from Sister A. Battistina; my husband took charge of this and wanted to have it done himself, so as to offer you this small consolation — together with his regards and respectful condolences.

Ah! dearest Mother, what a loss for you, for the Institute, and for me too, who felt as though covered by a shield through the prayers and counsel of this blessed soul! It now seems to me that you are doubly my Mother, and I would like to run to weep with you! My only comfort is the thought of the great glory she now enjoys, of her happiness with God, and that she will help us in a way even more powerful than on earth.

Dearest Mother, write to me, if you can; give me your precious news, and pray for one who needs it so much!

I embrace you with all my heart, kiss your hand, and ask your Holy Blessing.

Your most affectionate daughter in J. C.

Emilia

Forgive this so poorly written letter.

5. Letter of 6/13/1885 (AFSA G.4.33).

She relates that solemn funeral rites are being prepared for Sister Anna del Salvatore a week after her death; many people, to this end, make spontaneous offerings to express their admiration. The death of the Servant of God has left a great void in everyone.

Palermo, June 13, 1885

My dearest Mother,

I feel the need to write to you, not being able to have the comfort of being with you.

How is your precious health? How do you feel, my beloved Mother? I hope the Lord sustains you more than ever in this most painful trial, and that all the consolations and blessings of Heaven rain down upon you!

Preparations for the funeral have begun, and it is hoped the service will be beautiful and solemn. Many people have contributed to this end, and I believe the expenses will be covered by the offerings made out of the gratitude and admiration of all who had the good fortune to know this blessed soul.

Ah! my Mother, what a terrible emptiness we feel, the poor Sisters and I, but we also feel that our dear Superior prays for us!

If you knew how many lovely plans we used to make with dear Sister A[nna] Salvatore for the future, and if faith did not sustain me, I would believe everything lost and finished. [...]

I have gone twice to Casa Briuccia; the emptiness is terrible, but it is also a great consolation to see again these walls, witnesses to so much holiness and heroic virtue. I speak with the good Sisters, I weep with them, and nowhere else do I feel so great a peace as there.

Sunday, June 14.

Yesterday around 7 p.m. I went to the cemetery with Sister A. Macrina and Sister A. Corinna; we prayed at the dear tomb, and it was a great consolation for us.

For everything, dearest Mother, we thank you again for your telegram received this morning; I cannot express our gratitude and how dear and precious your blessings were to us. I too cannot think of your sorrow without a pang in my heart, but I hope that our dear departed one will think of us from Heaven, where she surely enjoys immense glory. Even still a pilgrim on earth, she obtained all from the Lord; how much more powerful will her prayers be now! [...]

Embracing you with all my heart and kissing your hand, I ask you, dearest Mother, to bless us both.

Your forever most affectionate daughter in J. C.

Emilia

6. Letter of 6/22/1885 (AFSA G.4.33).

She has spoken with Sister Anna Battistina, who described to her the red mark she saw on the heart of Sister Anna del Salvatore while tending to the body. She shows herself certain of the effective intercession of the Servant of God, and emphasizes her desire to remain hidden.

Palermo, June 22, 1885

My dearest Mother,

[...] Yesterday morning [Sister Anna Battistina] came to me and we spoke privately, as you have been kind enough to authorize me to do. Sister A. Battistina described to me the red mark on the heart which no one else saw but her, and surely the Lord allowed this to make it understood what great things would have been discovered in this heart, which burned with love for Him her whole life long. What a pity! that this inspiration came neither to Sister A. Battistina nor to the Confessor; it is clear that our most humble Superior wanted to hide herself even in the next life! I asked whether something could still be done, but the Superior says this could not be obtained, and I believe it too, because they are extremely strict in this regard. What a great pity! But we hope that the Lord, for His greater glory, will preserve everything, and will make the sanctity of his humble Spouse shine forth still more within a year. [...]

I imagine how you must feel the void left by our dear Superior, who would have given her life to please you. But you are right that from her blessedness she can obtain for us even more graces, and surely watches over us. How sad everything seems to me, though, without her, who was a star that guided me. The Sisters feel this great loss deeply, but have a strength that reveals the power of Sister A[nna] Salvatore's prayers. One can see that the Saints make one weep differently from others.

I embrace you with all my heart, my dearest Mother, and, kissing your hand, I ask you to bless me together with my husband. [...]

Your most grateful and affectionate daughter in J. C.

Emilia

7. Letter of 7/7/1885 (AFSA G.4.33).

A month has passed since the death of Sister Anna del Salvatore; she still recalls her goodness and charity. The Princess considers the Institute as a legacy left to her. She is certain of having a saint in heaven who prays for her.

Palermo, July 7, 1885

My dearest Mother,

[...] Today it is already a month since we lost our Superior; she enjoys the glory the Lord prepared for her, and this is the only comfort in the great sorrow of no longer having her with us. Though I should live a thousand years, I will always keep present her goodness, her charity, which she lavished on me with motherly affection, and I can do nothing more for her now except keep her memory in my heart, try to make myself less unworthy of her holy affection, and consider, in my small way, her daughters, the dear Institute, as a legacy she left me. Ah! my Mother, I express so poorly what I feel, but you will understand me. [...] And I hope, more than ever, to have the longed-for grace; I have a Mother who prays for me on earth and a saint who intercedes in Heaven, and although I have no merit at all, the Lord will let himself be appeased, oh how I hope so! [...]

I have obtained photographs of the Superior, and I take the pleasure of sending you two of them. What a beautiful expression; I never tire of looking at it, and I seem to read so many beautiful things in her gaze. [...]

My Mother, I commend myself to you still.

Your most devoted daughter in J. C.

Emilia

8. Letter of 7/20/1885 (AFSA G.4.33).

She recounts having been at Casa Briuccia, where she prayed gladly with the sisters; she sensed the absence/presence of Sister Anna del Salvatore, to whose intercession she attributes the help given to the Institute.

Palermo, July 20, 1885

My dearest Mother,

Each of your letters brings me a growing joy and consolation, but less and less am I able to express the deep gratitude and affection I feel so alive in my heart. [...]

I was at Casa Briuccia, and the Blessed Sacrament was exposed, and it was so sweet for me to pray among the Daughters of St. Anne; but how much our dear Sister A[nna] Salvatore is missed; yet one senses that she is near us.

With great consolation I hear of the infirmary for the Daughters of St. Anne. Sister A. Battistina tells me that Father Briuccia is very well disposed; may God be praised for it! Sister A[nna] Salvatore surely looks after it, and we may hope for great help for the Institute through her prayers. [...]

I embrace you with all my heart, my dearest Mother; pray to the Lord that he soon grant me the consolation of doing so in person. Ah! how I long for it! Kissing your hand, I ask your blessing, and I am forever

Your most affectionate daughter in J. C.

Emilia

9. Letter of 8/2/1885 (AFSA G.4.33).

She feels the need for the help of Sister Anna del Salvatore, and expresses lively gratitude for the Servant of God.

Franzensbad, August 2, 1885

My dearest Mother,

[...] Since I have been traveling it seems to me a dream that our Sister A[nna] Salvatore is no more! How terrible this loss is! If only I could see her and hear her, at least in a dream; I have such need of her urgings! Ah! how much I owe her, if only I knew how to make the most of it.

I embrace you with all my soul, dearest Mother; I kiss your hand and ask you to commend us to the Lord and bless us.

Your most affectionate daughter

Emilia

10. Letter of 8/16/1885 (AFSA G.4.33).

To obtain a grace, she is making a nine-month novena to the Most Holy Trinity, following the advice Sister Anna del Salvatore gave her while she was still alive.

Franzensbad, August 16, 1885

My dearest Mother,

I cannot express to you with what joy and consolation I received your most precious letter. [...]

So far, my dearest Mother, there is nothing new for me, and it seems to me there will not be for the present.

Our dear Sister A[nna] Salvatore had told me that I must first become better, but as I have not become so, I cannot expect the grace right away. The late Superior had proposed to me, on her last return from Piacenza, that I make a nine-month novena to the Most Holy Trinity, which I began last May 1st, never failing to say it; perhaps, aided by your prayers, my dear Mother, and those of Sister A[nna] Salvatore, up there the Most Holy Virgin will deign to obtain it for me. [...]

Always commending myself to your prayers, I embrace you with all my heart, my most beloved Mother, and kiss your hand, imploring your blessing for us. My husband charges me with his most respectful regards, and I am

Your most affectionate daughter in J. C.

Emilia

d) Excerpts from the Depositions of some Witnesses in the "Gattorno" Process.

From the Summarium of the Positio super Virtutibus of Blessed Mother Rosa Gattorno: excerpts from the depositions of witnesses who speak of the Servant of God.

1. Mrs. Emilia Settimo, Princess of Fitalia (31st Witness in the Roman Ordinary Process, pp. 426-428).

In recounting how she came to know Mother Rosa Gattorno, the witness highlights her spiritual bond with Sister Anna del Salvatore, and the great esteem she held for her.

Before this acquaintance [with Mother Rosa Gattorno] I was on very friendly terms with Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, who died in the odor of sanctity, and of whom I was a great admirer. I spent long, most sweet hours with her, and for my spirit that acquaintance was enough, so much so that when at times Sister Anna del Salvatore said to me, "Oh, if only you knew the Mother General!" speaking to me of her holiness, I remained quite indifferent, because, I repeat, my spirit was satisfied with her conversation, and that was enough for me.

But when Mother Gattorno was about to come to Palermo, Sister Anna del Salvatore spoke to me about it with great enthusiasm, wishing that I too would come to know her. On her arrival, she herself introduced me to the Servant of God. I went in indifferent, but on seeing her for the first time, I had a great impression of majesty, as of a queen, of extraordinary authority and, at the same time, of great sweetness. Our conversation (which was the only one on that first visit of hers to Sicily) turned on a project of hers to found a Third Order of Daughters of St. Anne, a project that would extend also to men...

Sister A. del Salvatore, after this first acquaintance I made with the Servant of God, often returned to speak to me of it...

Until then, whenever the Servant of God came to Palermo, I thought, with regret, that I would not be able to spend time at ease with Sister A. del Salvatore. On this occasion my husband too was presented to the Servant of God, and he greeted her with the same reverence he used towards our Queen Mother, spontaneously, as I well noticed...

The visits went on following one another... until I came into intimacy, and this happened especially after the death of Sister A. del Salvatore.

2. His Most Reverend Eminence Gennaro Granito Di Belmonte440 (1st Witness in the Roman Ordinary Process, p. 38).

The witness, a highly qualified Eminence — confidant and spiritual director of Mother Rosa Gattorno — shows himself well informed about the sensible communications the Foundress had with Sister Anna del Salvatore after her death, and knows of her effective mediation before God.

The Servant of God [Mother Rosa Gattorno] also received from her Lord, from the Most Holy Virgin and from the Saints, sensible communications, as regarded her spirit, in answer to graces she asked for or doubts in which she found herself concerning her own spirit and her Institute [...]

In the sensible communications of which I have spoken, the Lord, the Virgin, and the Saints appeared to her personally, and the Lord also allowed her daughter, Sister Anna del Salvatore, who had died in the odor of sanctity, to appear to her visibly, to whom the Servant of God had turned as an intermediary before Him, and this one brought her the answer.

When the Servant of God spoke to me at times of these events, I absolutely exclude that she did so out of ostentation or vainglory.

3. Sister Anna Celsa Speranza (9th Witness in the Roman Ordinary Process, pp. 262-263; 268).

Through long experience beside the Foundress — whose Secretary and General Counselor she also was — and above all through the deep bond she lived with her, the witness reveals significant details about the special relationship between Mother Gattorno and Sister Anna del Salvatore.

If some Sister showed more special virtue and a greater spirit of sacrifice, as for instance Sister Anna Salvatore Orsi, she received some special consideration. Sister Anna Salvatore, too, however, had her trials first; but then, when it became known who Sister A. Salvatore was, the special consideration began. By this I mean that she kept vigil at night in prayer...

In April 1900, one day the Servant of God comes into the study while I was alone there; she sits down and leans on the table, because her illness was pulling her down greatly. At that time I was very worried about the future of the Institute. I saw that soon we would no longer have our venerated Mother; I foresaw the assaults the Barbiellini family would make on us, and I turned a thousand things over in my mind... All at once I hear the Servant of God murmuring..., I listen and hear her say: "Be calm; all will be well; have trust." "Yes, I am calm, O Mother," I answer her, "but I weep because I see you suffering so much. But these ills alone ought to be enough." Then the Servant of God turns to me and says: "You are not calm at all, and if I tell you so it is because I know it, and you cannot deny it to me. Be calm, then, I repeat to you, for all will go well; I have been assured that in the Secretariat everything is in order, and no one will ever be able to touch a hair of your heads: at the gates stands my Salvatore, who will protect you." Her Salvatore would have been Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, who died in June 1885 in the odor of sanctity, and whose Process has already begun in Palermo. The Servant of God, with those words, was reading my inmost thoughts, and they were a true prophecy, since the Barbiellini family, in the final days, indeed during the Servant of God's agony, were plotting to have seals placed everywhere, but despite this, and despite ten years of litigation, they were unable to do us any harm, or touch anything.

e) Various letters and reminiscences of Sister Anna Celsa Speranza

Under this heading are reproduced, in chronological order, 5 letters (or excerpts of them) and a passage from the Memoirs of Sister Anna Celsa Speranza (cf. below, p. 508), which dwell on the Servant of God's reputation for holiness.

1. Two letters of the superior Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi to the foundress Mother Rosa Gattorno (AFSA F.5.39/3).

a) Of 6/13/1885

She recounts in great detail the last earthly day of Sister Anna del Salvatore, whom she herself personally attended for many hours. The Servant of God was aware of her approaching death: she was serene and cheerful and continually repeated: "fiat." She herself asked for the Anointing of the Sick.

A. M. F.

My dearest Mother,

I have received a letter from Sister A. Benedetta and Celsa; they tell me I have not given news of Salvatore's death.

Here I am to tell you everything I was able to see on the 7th, the day of her death. In the morning I sent two sisters to get news, and they found her serene, content, telling the sisters: "let us begin to detach ourselves, to depart from this earth." Around one in the afternoon I went myself, and found Her Excellency the Princess of Fitalia there; they were preparing the enema ordered by the doctor to give a little relief and hope of life, and it was given in my presence. Around 3 the poor invalid asked for rest, and all the sisters were sent out, leaving only the one who served as nurse.

Around four the doctor came and found her a little relieved, but still she could not pass anything and have a bowel movement; the doctor said: "tonight an olive oil enema will be given: if that has no effect, a small operation will be done tomorrow morning"; but the sick woman remained serene, saying nothing about this; then the doctor told her she would recover and should take heart; she, as expansive as she always was, thanked the doctor for his care and for everything else; once the doctor had left, it slipped from her lips that she hoped not to undergo the small operation, all smiling, meaning that she would not reach that point, would not reach tomorrow.

I stayed until 4:30, and then went to the hospital for a meal, and returned in the evening after the Angelus, when she had already asked herself for the Holy Oil, which was given to her in full awareness. I went into the room and found her with a rattle, and grew suspicious; I withdrew; I said — that is, the Princess and the Monsignor asked me how she was; I said she would not live until morning, that that rattle would suffocate her, as indeed happened. So I placed myself at her right side and did not leave her until her last breath, and those 3 hours I spent at her side were of true consolation because of the joy she showed, both in words and with smiles. Every minute she took hold of her Crucifix and kissed it, pressing it close; the confessor, who never left her, would say to her from time to time: "Salvatore, remember Jesus and Mary." "Yes, Father." And then always her word Fiat; then she felt herself dying, and asked to be allowed to get down; I said to her: "Salvatore, you cannot, see how very unwell you feel"; she said: "for charity's sake, let me"; and we, with words, tried to persuade her. "Very well," I told her, "Superior, obey, because it will do you harm if you get down." She said nothing more, and remained so for more than half an hour, then asked: "Father, will you grant it to me, for charity's sake?" Then I said to her: "but do you need to?" She: "Yes." So everyone withdrew, and she was helped down, and it seemed she wanted to rest. I, fearing something, said: "Salvatore, be good, go to bed"; she: "at once."

Around 10:30 the Princess wanted to take her leave, but did not have the courage to speak, and asked me to tell her; I spoke up and said: "Superior, the Princess wishes to go, and bids you farewell." The said Princess knelt down, saying to her: "Mother, do you promise to be my guide with your counsel also in heaven?" The poor dying woman said: "Yes, Princess." She added: "make me the usual little cross on my forehead." And the poor sick woman, with a trembling hand, amid everyone's tears, made the cross on the forehead of her dear Princess, taking leave with a handclasp and a smile, a sign of never seeing her again. Meanwhile the hour drew near. I said to the confessor: "it would be good to give her a recommendation for everyone, first the Mother, then the Institute and the Sisters"; he said: "we will do that." A few minutes pass and the confessor said to her: "Superior, I want a promise." "Yes, Father." "To remember before the Lord the Mother, her Institute, the good Sisters; will you do this?" "Yes, Father, yes." Then he let her rest a little; the confessor returned to say to her: "Superior, the sisters want a keepsake, what do you say, before leaving don't you want to tell us anything? Say something to remember you by." In three gasps of breath, because she could no longer manage, she said: "Let them be good." The confessor then said to her: "do you want to give them your blessing, which they so desire?" She, fully ready, yet making a sign that the Father should give it on her behalf, wanting to raise her hand but unable to. After this she wanted to get down, that is, she asked to, but it was not allowed, and she said: "for charity's sake let me get down!" I then said: "be good, see how much you suffer by getting down, bear with this desire of yours, but do the Lord's will." She gave herself over, saying Fiat, the last word from her mouth. A moaning began, leaving the rattle behind; I said to the Father: "let us say the Litanies." He began the Litanies, and had not reached halfway when her beautiful soul expired. Before expiring she gathered her Crucifix with her hands in the form of a cross. She expired at 11 o'clock at night on the 7th of this month, amid the weeping of everyone, which was pitiful to see.

As soon as she expired, the Sisters appointed to dress her set to work; I stayed watching a little how they did it, and also because I could not tear myself away from that holy body. While the Sisters were removing her shift, I glimpsed in passing a mark beneath the heart; however, I made no move at all, but remained uncertain; it was a mark three fingers wide and nine centimeters long. At that moment I felt my heart pound, almost wanting to verify what it was, but a fear held me back in front of the Sisters, fearing to seem too curious; but once day had come I took courage and said to the confessor: "I saw something on the Superior, but I don't know if I saw wrong," and told him what had happened. He told me: "you go and have all the Sisters leave, and look." Which indeed I did, and I lifted her shift without undressing her completely: yes, the said mark was like this: the flesh reddened, as when one applies, I cannot explain myself, so many small red dots, but the skin was the same, only the redness appeared; I do not know what it could have been, I only let myself be overcome by curiosity in order to make known what I had seen; what I can tell you, Mother, is that one could not tear oneself away from her body, such was the good one felt just from looking at it.

Now let me tell you of the weeping; I, with a Sister, at midnight went to fetch [illegible word follows] a cordial, because it was truly agonizing; there were myself, the Father Confessor, and Sister Clemente, taking turns tending to one or another, not knowing what to do. Around one o'clock I took Sister Fabiana to the Fernandes Infirmary, because it would have been the death of her to keep her there where the dead Sister lay, and I returned to Briuccia, where I stayed until she was accompanied to burial on the evening of the 8th. The whole day, what desolation for everyone! While in the evening we were setting out to accompany Salvatore, behold a messenger came to call Alfonsina, with the confessor, because Gualberta was unwell. Alfonsina goes to the house, and we, on returning, went to the little hospital to attend Gualberta, who died at 11 at night on the 8th. See this, Mother: well, while Sister Gualberta was dying, a peace was felt in all of us, even though it was the second [death] coming so soon; and yet such a peace that one could only believe it a miracle of Salvatore; all of us attributed it to her. Mother, to tell you everything I would have to speak to you in person. I hope to have this grace.

Now let me tell you, Mother, that I have gone to the Sisters every day, but I keep returning to the Hospital, because to leave it we need to have the Parish Priest speak to the Commissioner so as not to upset him, you understand me, Mother; I will do whatever you command me, but, Mother, I fear I am not doing my proper duty, and up to this moment I have not even told the sisters, because until one has spoken with Sichilone... Nor have I wanted the sisters to hear the letters read. The Parish Priest will arrive from the countryside around the 18th of this month, but let me tell you, Mother, be assured it is no burden to us; I do not yet fully know the inner workings of the house, but as far as I can see there is nothing wrong; I will write to you more clearly about it when things are clearer. Two sisters have been sent off so far, it is hoped. On Monday I thought of sending off Patrocinio, because she had a fever, it could not be done. Alberica is out of danger; it is hoped the ones in quarantine will recover: it is hoped that in a few days they will come home.

Mother, the funeral will be held on Monday, in the Chapel. There will be Masses continuously until 10, then the sung Mass.

As for the rest, Mother, the Hospital is getting along so-so; when the Parish Priest arrives the Contract will be drawn up. Sichilone is no longer as he was before; truly the manner of Father Pizzoli has converted him, and everything has worked out. Enough, it is all the Lord who works.

Mother, I am finishing because I am tired, and send greetings in the name of all the Sisters and of the Parish Priest, who wrote to me to convey his condolences; weeping and praying, he asks to bless us all, and I remain always yours

most humble daughter

Sister A. Battistina

Palermo, 6/13/1885

b) Of 6/15/1885

The service of suffrage for Sister Anna del Salvatore has just ended: the attendance was very great, and the funeral eulogy will be sent to print. The Servant of God greatly loved the Lord, from whom she will be able to obtain many graces; and already a special protection is manifesting itself.

A. M. F.

My dearest beloved Mother,

Last year [1885] good God took away the beautiful soul of Sister Anna Francesca Savignone, who by her example was an edification to all who came near her. But a sharper dart, a greater loss, God allowed the good Mother to suffer this year, by taking from her the dearest of her Sisters when she least expected it. The almost sudden death of Sister Anna del Salvatore, provincial of Sicily, which occurred on June 7, 1885, filled the whole Institute with the deepest grief. This gem of a sister was a great support for the dear Mother, for she governed all the houses of Sicily, eighteen in number, admirably, and by her example and her words knew so well how to keep alive in them the spirit of the Institute and the observance of the holy rules, so as to form the glory of the Institute itself.

God worked many wonders through this servant of his. Indeed, we have the house of the infirmary sisters, which at the beginning of its founding had no small share of suffering. Entrusted wholly to Providence, the poor sisters often lacked even the necessities, and led their lives with great hardship. Our heroine, from morning to night, went about seeking subscriptions and donations; and so many good people of Palermo were won over by her virtues that in a short time the neglected and poor house of the infirmary sisters was transferred to a sumptuous apartment in the Briuccia Palace, one of the city's principal palaces, and provided for beyond its needs. So many blessings of God and so much providence, from where did they come if not from the life of self-denial and sacrifice of Sister Anna del Salvatore? Oh, blessed are you! who now enjoy the reward of your many long sufferings, in the beautiful Paradise, in the sight of your spouse Jesus!

I will leave off describing here all the particulars of this chosen soul, since her biography will be printed separately, and afterwards her life. The author, Onorata Colli, a lay teacher from Piacenza, very close to the foundress Mother Rosa Gattorno and her Institute from its origins, describes in abundant detail — having personally known the Servant of God — the life and path of holiness of "this great soul" (as she was called by Mother Rosa Gattorno herself).
