Historical Notes on the Life of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi

professed religious of the Order of the Daughters of St. Anne

dedicated to Her Excellency Princess Emilia di Fitalia

Declaration

In conformity with the decrees of Urban VIII of March 13, 1625, and of June 5, 1631, as well as with the Decrees of the Sacred Congregation of Rites, we solemnly declare that to all the favors and wonders narrated here we intend to attribute only human faith, so as not to anticipate the authoritative judgment of Holy Church.

Preface

To instruct men, example is more effective than words. This is an incontestable truth, which the Divine Master put into practice when, preaching humility, charity, resignation, forgiveness of offenses, and all the other holy Maxims, he chose to live poor, to heal the sick, to console the afflicted, to submit in resignation to the will of his Father, who, for the salvation of mankind, had condemned him, an innocent victim, to die, and in dying forgave from the Cross those who had made of his body the cruelest butchery.

On the basis, then, of this truth, there is proposed to the Daughters of St. Anne the life of one of their sisters, Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, so that they, imitating the virtues of which this good soul gave so luminous an example, may, like her, acquire such merits before God as to be called, one day, to enjoy Eternal Blessedness.

The dedication of these Historical Notes to Her Excellency Princess Emilia di Fitalia has the purpose of attesting to this Illustrious Lady the high esteem and lively gratitude the Institute feels for Her, who was one of the most affectionate and devoted persons to Sister Anna del Salvatore, holding for her that veneration one can hold for a great and holy soul.

May the Illustrious Princess be pleased to accept this humble homage, and remember always that the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne is glad and considers itself honored by the benevolence which She deigns to grant it, and may She be assured that the chosen soul of Sister Anna del Salvatore will always hover about Her, to protect and defend her against the ills of life.

I. Birth, Childhood, and Youth of Marianna Orsi

In the district of Borgotaro, in the Diocese of Piacenza and the Province of Parma, lies Albareto. It is situated in the Gotra valley, precisely on the right bank of this stream, which flows from South to North, and because of its location, the pleasantness of the place, and the healthful air that blows there, it is justly considered one of the most delightful spots in the valley.

And it was in this town that, in the year 1842, on February 23, Marianna Orsi came into the world, the chosen creature whose praises I shall humbly weave, if God wills to favor me with his help.

She was the firstborn of nine siblings, three girls and six boys, whom the parents, Angelo and Domenica Mussi, sought to raise in a Christian manner, for, being good Catholics, they took care that their children grow up in the holy fear of God.

It is difficult, not to say impossible, to imagine the joy with which those excellent parents welcomed the coming into the world of this little creature, the first fruit of their lawful union. They were not troubled by the thought that the family was growing and expenses increasing, as very often happens to those who are poor and see the joy of the happy moment disturbed by the vague fear of perhaps not being able afterwards to provide all that is necessary for the life of the newborn child. They were of comfortable means, and so had the wherewithal to meet the expenses of maintaining the growing family.

At home, then, there was great celebration when, the day after her birth, the baby girl was carried to the holy font that would wash her of original sin. She was baptized by the Very Reverend Don Giovanni Maestri, Rector of that Parish, and had as her godfather her uncle Francesco Mussi, then Podestà of Albareto, and as her godmother her aunt Giovanna Orsi, and was given the sweet name of Marianna.

But if the father was content at the birth of his firstborn, the mother could not restrain her joy, so great was it, and she made it known to the relatives and friends who came to visit her, telling everyone that she was fully happy and that nothing more remained for her to desire here below. Did the pious mother have a presentiment of to what high degree of perfection the soul of that poor little creature wailing at her side, in need of everything, would one day rise? Had her mother's heart divined what greatness was sheltered in that tender little body, which awaited from her breast all it needed to grow and develop, and which, without her loving care, would surely have perished? I truly could not say; I know, however, that the birth of this child brought the parents a joy so great that they themselves could never explain it, and which they certainly did not feel again at the coming into the world of any other child of their numerous offspring.

Marianna's infancy was like that of all good little girls. Always attached to her mother, as the rose is to its stem, she lived by her mother's life. Of a sweet and yielding nature, she bent easily to the will of others, and in her well-formed little heart she felt no envy when her mother was obliged to share with the little brothers and sisters born after her the care that before had been entirely devoted to her.

When, in 1846, she was admitted to receive, in the Parish Church of Borgotaro, from His Most Reverend Excellency Monsignor Michele Angelo Orlandi, Bishop of Pontremoli, the Holy Sacrament of Confirmation, it was a truly extraordinary event for the little girl, barely four years old, and although she had not yet reached the age of reason, still, by the devotion with which she presented herself to receive this Sacrament, she gave clear signs of understanding its full importance.

Attending assiduously to the explanations of Christian Doctrine which the good Parish Priest gave his little parishioners every Sunday, and heeding the teachings of her most pious parents, she was instructed early and well in the Catechism, so that she deserved, also for the good sense she showed, to be admitted, young as she still was, to the Sacred Eucharistic Table.

The day of her First Communion was a day of blessedness for her. She already felt drawn towards her Divine Spouse, who was afterwards to be the treasure, the comfort, the hope of her candid soul. To be edified by it, one had to see with what devotion the singular child, kneeling with her little hands joined, awaited the Priest bringing the Sacred Host to her lips, trembling from inward emotion! Other young girls had shared with her in this heavenly grace, but on no other face could be seen, as on hers, the burning desire to possess Jesus and the strong fear of being unworthy to host the King of kings.

O Lord, how great you are in your works! Slowly and secretly you know how to make the little plants sprout that will one day give your Church the most exquisite and abundant fruits!

Following the example of her family, Marianna grew up very religious; she heard Holy Mass daily, attended the sermons and the Divine Offices, and exercised herself, as much as her age allowed, in all the works of Charity towards God and neighbor. These religious practices did not, however, keep her from helping her mother with the housework, in which she always showed herself ready for any task. But it was especially in the care of her little brothers and sisters that she displayed her activity and insight, for her mother, called to other matters in running the household, very often entrusted them entirely to her. With what love she watched over them! With what self-denial she gave up amusing herself with the other girls her age, in order to stay with them! How patient she was in bearing their whims, and how attentive to satisfying their lawful wishes! And when they fell into faults for which the mother would have been obliged to inflict some punishment, there was the affectionate sister defending them against the mother's just severity, asking forgiveness for them, offering herself as guarantor of their future conduct. And since in her keen discernment she well understood that nothing is more harmful in the raising of children than ill-advised pity and indulgence, thus she, with the good sense she had, while acting as advocate for her little brothers and sisters before her mother, became for them a strict judge when, alone with them, she did her duty by admonishing them for those very faults for which she had just a moment before begged forgiveness.

In those times, elementary education for women among the common people had not yet been provided for in country villages by means of public schools, so that in Albareto too, lacking anyone to instruct the village women, very few could be found who knew how to read and write. Among this small number, however, was Marianna, who had her own father as teacher. She was not, then, like so many other poor girls, her fellow villagers, entirely without instruction, and being gifted as she was with much intelligence, she would no doubt have made progress along the path of study, had she had the opportunity and the time to devote to it.

But her family needed her work. Her brothers Luigi and Giovanni, now grown somewhat older, were admitted as day students to the Seminary of Bedonia, and Marianna had to follow them there, to prepare their food, look after their linens, see to the cleaning of the house, and guide them, while their mother, in Albareto, saw to governing the rest of the large family.

Having fulfilled this duty, she acceded to the wish of her uncles Don Antonio and Don Luigi Mussi, the former parish priest of Buzzò, the latter of Rovinaglia, going now to one, now to the other, to lend her service in the good running of the household; but however well she got on with her uncles, by whom she was held in the regard she deserved, she could not grow accustomed to being apart from her mother and family, and decided to return to Albareto.

Our Marianna was much loved by the whole village for the rare gifts with which she was adorned. She had a very gentle nature and a calm spirit; she was without vanity in dress and bearing; she did not know what pretense was, and though she liked to be in the cheerful company of girls her own age, she was nonetheless most reserved in conduct, and in conversation never let slip a word that was less than proper. Among her good qualities shone blind obedience to her parents, to her relatives, and to whoever looked after her soul, and respect towards everyone.

The seeds of religious feeling had put down deep roots in her; and so she attended with admirable devotion to the Holy Sacraments, and consecrated to God the hours her household duties left free. On novenas and feast days she hurried eagerly to church, just as she hurried promptly to the ringing of the bell that called the faithful to accompany the Holy Viaticum to some sick person, or the bearing of a poor deceased person to their final resting place.

Angelo Orsi's family had grown too large; to raise it, debts had had to be incurred, so that, to pay them off and to seek elsewhere the earnings that were lacking in Albareto, the good man decided in 1863 to sell his property and to go live in Centuèra, in the territory of Piacenza, with the whole family, except for Marianna, who remained in her native village in the home of her uncles Francesco and Lorenzo Mussi as housekeeper, where, thanks to her goodness, she was loved and respected. Marianna remained in Albareto another three years, then returned to her family and stayed there until, called by God to the cloistered life, she aspired to nothing else but to fulfill her desire.

And it is precisely for this reason that, even when obliged, so as not to lack in good manners and courtesy, to accept an invitation to some family celebration at the home of friends or relatives, she would return home displeased and regretful, so much so as to weep over it when alone in the silence of her little room. It is also for this reason that, if at one time she had allowed some hope to be formed in a person who, drawn by her fine qualities, had asked her parents for her hand in marriage, she, enlightened by a higher Grace, had afterwards withdrawn her word, saying she no longer wished to marry, because she felt inclined to become a nun. She did desire a spouse, yes, but one who would be always handsome, always young, always loving for all eternity. And of what spouse did she mean to speak, if not of Jesus Christ?

Our Marianna, born and raised in a most religious family, could not help but breathe in its excellent principles along with the air. Her father had three brothers and an uncle who were priests, and a sister a nun among the Oblates of St. James in Pontremoli. She, then, inclined by nature to dedicate herself wholly to the Lord, heard with joy the mysterious voice that invited her to abandon the world, and let herself be led by it to the door of that Institute, of which, through her outstanding virtues, she was to be, as will be seen further on, its glory and splendor.

II. Marianna Enters the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne

From what has been set out in the preceding chapter, we know that Marianna had rejoined her family in Centuèra, which, now going through grave hardship, had to submit to sacrifices and privations never before endured. But being religious and Christian as it was, the excellent family bore the new state with resignation, trusting always in the help of Divine Providence, which would surely not abandon them. Marianna, showing herself on every occasion a good, loving, and submissive daughter, sought to ease her family's sufferings through love, diligence at work, and by keeping the household mood always cheerful, even when the hardships they lived in would have made her shed bitter tears. Inwardly, however, she grieved at the thought that her father, her mother, and her siblings were in distress. As for herself, she had grown accustomed to eating the coarsest food, and was even seen eating chicken feed, potatoes, and rotten fruit, on the pretext that they were good for her stomach. Most fervent, then, were the prayers she raised to God, that He would improve her family's condition, from which she would soon, by an irresistible force, have to part forever.

In her work and in the silence of prayer, the mysterious voice, which had already suggested to her that she consecrate herself wholly to God, kept speaking to her soul in sweet tones of heavenly things, and making her fall ever more in love with the cloistered life, where she could enter into closer communion with Him who was now her only aspiration. Oh, how she longed to be able to bid farewell to the world and all its vain allurements, to embrace that state which would more easily lead her to the possession of that eternal, sole, and infinite Good, by which she felt herself repeatedly called! And with this most vivid desire she waited anxiously for God to dispose of her, so as to conform herself wholly to His Holy Will, which she would ever bless!

Marianna was then twenty years old, and it was by the Lord's disposition that, having made known to a trusted person her intention of entering an Institute where she could devote herself to the care of the sick, she was pointed towards that of the Daughters of St. Anne, then newly founded. Now she knew the refuge where she could spend her life praying and doing good; it remained for her to know whether she had truly been called there by the Lord, or whether her inclinations were not the fruit of an overwrought mind, and she submitted herself, on her own, to the test. Should she emerge victorious against the world's allurements, she would be convinced that hers was a true vocation.

She was not spared, during her trial period within her family, the strongest temptations; the world called to her with its many distractions; now it was cheerful and handsome young men who worked to turn her from her holy purpose, putting before her eyes how beautiful life is, and that it is foolish to quench, at twenty, in the most joyful and smiling age, the most ardent affections of the heart. Now it was lively and attractive companions who, going to church on feast days, passed before her, beautiful in their finery, and tried to tempt her to imitate them, making herself, like them, attractive so as to please. And that poor soul, swept up in the whirlwind of temptations, like a fragile little boat amid the waves of a stormy sea, struggled against everything and everyone, by dint of fasting, mortifications of every kind, and prayers, to obtain from Heaven those graces she needed in order to emerge victorious and acquire the lights that were to guide her in the choice of her state in life.

Heaven granted her the help she sought, and when she felt quite firm in her resolve, when she understood that the mysterious voice calling her to the cloister was the Lord's, she set out her unchanging intention to her family. This, at first, showed itself displeased with such a decision, coming at an inconvenient time, for at home Marianna was needed, this active and good daughter; but the young woman's entreaties were so many, and the religious feeling in that exemplary family so strong, that in the end she was granted what she anxiously desired.

On November 4, then, of the year 1868, that is barely three years after the founding of the Order of the Daughters of St. Anne, the good daughter left, in tears, the family to which she had given examples of the finest virtues; and, blessed by her sorrowing parents and uncles, she departed from her little village to enter another family, to which, if not by the bonds of kinship, she would be bound by the feeling of observance of the constitutions, a feeling that would lead her to recognize in her Superiors the supreme authority of God, and in the other members so many sisters, the former deserving veneration and blind and prompt obedience, the latter deserving boundless esteem and fraternal affection.

III. Marianna's Postulancy

And now the pious young woman's wishes were fulfilled; now she was dead to the world, to live with the sole aim of loving her beloved Spouse. For a long time she had aspired to nothing else, and having entered the Cloister, she directed all her actions towards making herself worthy of the grace God had granted her, placing her in a position where she had to think of nothing but the sanctification of her own soul. "My Jesus, my Jesus," she must surely have exclaimed in the secret of her soul, "I am unworthy of so great a grace! I am a poor sinner, and you mercifully stretch out your hand to me, to raise me to the rank of sister of your most loving Mother. Yes, soon, I hope, I shall be a Daughter of St. Anne, and grant that I may never prove unworthy of this immense benefit of yours." Meanwhile, good Marianna showed herself ready to do everything that would be required of her during the period of testing.

Accustomed to obeying her parents, she had no trouble obeying the Mistress of Novices. She knew that God had chosen her Mistress to represent Him, and to be the instrument through which His Holy Will was made known to her, and she held every word of hers as sacred, and would not have drawn back even before the gravest obstacle when she had to carry out an order of hers, which for her was inviolable law; she obeyed, then, always obeyed without regret and without complaint, indeed glad to be able to give her Superiors proof of her perfect submission.

But obedience was not the only virtue Marianna showed during her postulancy; she possessed others, certainly no less admirable than the first. I shall try to give a sketch of all of them, to show that the Lord grants his chosen ones special graces, by which they can serve as an example and edification to others.

There was no task, however menial, that she did not take on without feeling any reluctance, and with an always serene spirit. She considered herself inferior to all her companions, and so spoke to them humbly, and welcomed with gratitude every correction. If it happened that in doing this or that thing she made a mistake, she immediately blamed it on her own ignorance and begged anyone at all to give her suggestions. And when it fell to her to give them to others, she did so with such delicate discretion that no one felt humiliated. When the Mistress gave her some task of a certain importance, in accepting it she never failed to beg her first to choose someone more capable than herself; and let no one think she did this out of affected humility, or to free herself from the obligation: no, she was truly convinced that she was the most ignorant and unfit of all the young women with her in the postulancy, and it grieved her to accept a task that another would have known how to carry out far better than she. And if, afterwards, her pleas were not heeded, not trusting in her own strength, she prostrated herself at the foot of the altar to beg help from God, to whom alone she gave the glory, if she managed to satisfy the wishes of her Superiors.

But the fine qualities of obedience and humility, of which we have spoken, were joined in our Marianna to that of charity, which uplifts the soul and makes it taste the purest and holiest satisfactions. Yes, she loved Jesus in all those who, through illness or for some other reason, needed help; and one cannot express the sorrow she felt when she learned that one of the postulants, or some sister, was ill. What a distinguished grace it would have been for her to be allowed to stay at the bedside of the sick woman, to care for her and never leave her alone, by day or by night! And how many times she had begged for this grace without ever being able to obtain it, because the office of nurse was entrusted to others who were already professed sisters! If she saw a companion sad, melancholy, weeping at the thought of her distant family, of the past, of the future, she drew near to her solicitously and, with gentle manner, consoled her, speaking to her of the life of paradise that awaited her, of the comfort she would later find in serving Jesus; and she advised her to seek in fervent prayer the means of driving away sadness. How happy the pious young woman was if her words restored peace to her companion! On the other hand, what sorrow she felt when she found herself forced to mourn the loss of some companion who, not knowing how to fight against the first obstacles placed by the devil, returned to the world, where she would afterwards have to suffer the bitterest disillusionments. Nor was her charity limited to this alone; she had an excuse for everyone else's faults, while being most strict with her own, and never said a word that sounded like censure of another's conduct, or gossip. "Everyone is good, kind, and holy, except me, who am very wicked." This is a phrase she often repeated, and which clearly shows to what height the spirit of charity and humility of our Marianna rose, who within the walls of the blessed House that had welcomed her, in work and in prayer, had found that peace and happiness she had longed for so long.

To her too, however, as to all chosen souls, the minister of evil showed himself under various aspects, and the poor girl was not spared the most fearsome temptations. Now it was the thought of her parents, from whose support she had, by her work, taken away one means of sustenance, which invited her to return to the family; now it was the friends left behind in her village, who appeared before her cheerful and glad, to lead her back to the free life of the country; now it was the doubt of not being able afterwards to fulfill all the obligations of her state, which left her uncertain, hesitant; and now she grew frightened at the idea of eternal damnation, which she would have deserved had she not done the much, indeed the too much, that monastic life would demand of her. In vain did the devil labor in his malice and treachery to defeat her; God's grace was with her, and when temptations assailed her most strongly, she trustingly called upon the Protector of the weak and oppressed, and from Him obtained the strength needed to struggle bravely until she emerged victorious. Yes, she always triumphed, and after the triumph her soul could taste that serenity which comes from confidence in the Lord's help and from the awareness of having done what was possible so that evil would not triumph.

Thanks, then, to her good qualities, truly singular, Marianna had drawn upon herself the attention of her Superiors, who did not fail to subject her to the hardest trials, to be fully assured of her firm vocation. To this end they did not spare her severe reproofs even for faults of slight consequence, to which she responded with the most amiable apologies and the promise never again to fall into similar faults, and to be very careful not to commit others. They did not fail to subject her to relatively heavy work, to let her know that the Daughters of St. Anne do not live only a contemplative life but also an active one, and that they must therefore be prepared to bear the heavy toils that their mission as nurses requires. They accustomed her to practicing poverty, teaching her that she owned nothing, that everything necessary for her sustenance came to her from Providence, and that she therefore had no right to waste even the smallest part of it. They put her in a position to be able to relieve the miseries of poor sick people, training her to give them the necessary care. And she, willingly submitting to the trial, blessed her Superiors, towards whom she felt filled with the liveliest gratitude. "Without the hammer, iron would not be shaped," she used to say, "and I am just like a piece of iron; one must strike and strike to shape me."

Always seeking to fulfill her duties scrupulously, Marianna spent some months in the postulancy; and when the Reverend Mother Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno judged that the time had come to allow her to put on the religious habit, she called her to herself and gave her the happy news. It is easier to imagine than to describe the joy Marianna felt at this: she wept and laughed at once, she seemed beside herself. She then prostrated herself, without uttering a word, for joy had left her speechless, at the feet of the Mother, and, when she could speak, with the most moving words attested her own gratitude, promising her that she would always be devoted and faithful, and that she would always do all she could to make herself worthy of the grace that had been granted her.

Oh, what supreme joy! Soon she would see her hopes realized; soon she would put on that habit by which she would be marked with the sweet name of Daughter of St. Anne. She would go to the bedside of the languishing sick, open her arms to the forsaken little orphan, and speak words of comfort and resignation to the sorrowing, thus practicing the charity the Divine Master taught by word and by example. And in these sweet thoughts she attended to the preparations for her clothing, savoring in advance the joy of being able to say to her Jesus: "Beloved Spouse, now I am wholly yours; ah, make me worthy to possess you."

IV. Clothing and Novitiate of Sister Anna del Salvatore

The dawn of March 28, 1869 had broken, and Marianna, who in the longing of her desire had not closed her eyes all night, greeted with joy the most beautiful day of her life. With prayers and mortification she had prepared herself to receive the Holy Veil, and now she awaited, trembling, the solemn ceremony that, declaring her dead to the world, would open to her the way to the acquisition of the Infinite Good, which formed the most ardent desire of her fervent soul.

Now the candles are burning, now the Community has gathered in the Chapel awaiting the solemn moment, and Marianna, trembling with emotion, confused with humility, presents herself at the foot of the altar, where, renouncing the world and its pomps, she also renounces her baptismal name and takes that of Sister Anna del Salvatore. And behold the new Daughter of St. Anne who, all in tears, intones the Te Deum with her fellow sisters; behold the new servant of God, borne on the wings of thought and desire to Heaven, and in this sweet ecstasy of hers sees Jesus smiling at her and holding out his arms. "O Jesus, my Savior," she exclaims, "ah, grant that I may never become unworthy of the name just now given me! Grant that I may learn from You obedience, chastity, poverty, humility, and all those other virtues I need to persevere in goodness! Bless, O my Jesus, this creature, more imperfect than the worm of the earth, and allow me to follow in all and through all your Holy Will!"

The sacred ceremony is over, and Sister Anna del Salvatore leaves the Chapel with her fellow sisters, and gives free vent to her inward joy, going now to one, now to another, to speak of her happiness. By now she had obtained what she had longed for, for so long, and trusted in God's help in order to continue the journey still remaining to her, to reach the end of her pilgrimage, without letting herself be overcome by the snares of the devil, always ready to set them in order to snatch a soul away from the Lord.

Sister Anna del Salvatore entered the Novitiate, and her first care was to devote herself with all diligence to an exact knowledge of those holy Rules that were to guide her in her conduct. In this sweet peace, in work and in prayer, she passed her days serenely; but alas! a strong doubt assails her: will she be able to fulfill everything the holy Rules require of her? Do they not ask a bit too much? And by not observing the holy Rules in their full extent, would she not surely have earned eternal damnation! Why had she wanted to create greater difficulties for herself in gaining Paradise? One could earn eternal salvation even living in the world. The chosen spirits were not all priests, friars, and nuns; therefore... Had she returned to her family, how gladly her own would have welcomed her! And why did she not go back? She had not pronounced an indissoluble vow, so she was free to leave; and yet she still hesitated?... Yes, the good Novice hesitated, because, understanding that these temptations came to her from the devil, the executioner of souls, she wanted to fight energetically against him by opposing to his perverse suggestions an infinite number of good reasons. She did not love staying in the world, and had abandoned it of her own will; she was not sorry for the step she had taken, but rather thanked the Lord for having so inspired her. The holy Rules were not, no, too strict; rather they were very mild; a little good will and zeal would suffice, and she would find it easy to observe them in every point. In return for some slight sacrifice in combating her passions, she would afterwards enjoy peace of mind, would taste the joy of being able to serve Jesus in the person of the poor sick, would be able to converse more intimately with her heavenly Spouse, and for her soul eternal salvation would thereby be made easier. Strengthened by these considerations, Sister Anna del Salvatore overcame the diabolical temptations, by which perhaps a spirit less strong than hers would have been overcome, and was able to devote herself wholly to doing all that her new state required of her.

There was never a more zealous, prudent, sincere, humble, patient, tireless, and chaste novice than she. Never an act, never a word that betrayed the innocence of her heart, still untouched by any human malice. The will of the Mistress was sacred to her, a wish was a command; so that also in the novitiate, as before in the postulancy, she obeyed, always obeyed with a smile on her lips and contentment in her heart, whatever she was told to do. She would have gone to any lengths to make herself useful to the Institute which, as she herself often said in her outpourings of gratitude, had given her life.

She loved prayer, and felt particularly inflamed with love for Jesus. When she was in the presence of the Most Blessed Sacrament, she saw and heard nothing more of what was happening around her, and, had she been allowed, she would have remained kneeling at the foot of the altar day and night, without taking either food or rest.

When ordered, according to the Institute's purpose, to attend day or night to some poor sick person, Sister Anna del Salvatore felt such joy that she knew no other way to express it than by declaring herself most grateful to the Superiors from whom the order came. She was not frightened by the distress and squalor of the hovel where, deprived of the smallest comfort, she had to spend the hours she would otherwise have devoted, in Community, to quiet occupations or to rest. The thought that, by caring for the sick, she served Jesus, made her insensible to suffering and discomfort. And so she was always the first to ask to be sent on vigil; and she grieved when her Superiors, out of charity, prevented her, fearing for her health, from going out too often to attend the sick. With what fear, with what patience, with what humility she rendered to her patients the services they needed. And how many consoling words she said to them, so that they would accept with resignation the trial to which God had wished to subject them, to make them worthy of Heaven! At the bedside of the sick, Sister Anna del Salvatore was an Angel, and as such the poor sufferers regarded her, receiving from her spiritual and material comfort.

In the fulfillment of each of her duties the good Novice found the means of advancing in those virtues without which she certainly could not have risen to the degree of perfection she later attained. Though still very young, she showed herself endowed with extraordinary good sense. Her conduct, irreproachable in every respect, her practical skill in the good running of household affairs, her spirit of thrift did not go unnoticed by the Mother, who, endowed with keen discernment, was coming to the idea of making use of Sister Anna del Salvatore for the good of one of the Houses then being opened, and she did not delay in putting this idea into practice, almost certain that the sister would not belie the favorable expectations the Superiors had formed of her.

V. Sister Anna del Salvatore Leaves the Novitiate, by Order of the Reverend Mother Gattorno, to Go and Lend Her Service in a Recently Founded House

If whoever reads me knows the Rules that govern the Order of the Daughters of St. Anne today, Rules that require of the Novice a year of novitiate before she may take on any office that would take her away from the House where she is appointed to undergo her trial, may ask me: Why was Sister Anna del Salvatore exempted from following this law? Why did she pass from the Mother House in Piacenza to another before finishing the prescribed novitiate? Let the kind reader be so good as to go with me in thought back to the early days of the Institute, and he will find the answer to his questions.

In the year 1865 [sic, for 1866] the Order of the Daughters of St. Anne was founded in Piacenza, having as its purpose the care of the sick and the instruction and education of girls. But few knew of the founding of this Order, which came to life in a modest and quiet provincial town, without the pomp of advance notices or clamorous announcements, and the few who did know gave it no credence, as almost always happens with things whose appearance in the world is anything but extraordinary. It is thus no wonder that, at first, the number of those asking to join the religious Family was small. It was not long, however, before people of good sense understood the great benefit this Institute would bring to society, and so various towns began to request the generous work of the Daughters of St. Anne, to relieve the poor sick through free home care and care in hospitals, and to instruct children in nursery schools and elementary schools. The requests increase every day, and Mother Anna Rosa Gattorno raises from the depths of her soul the liveliest thanks to the Lord.

There is an urgent need for personnel; nurses, teachers, and superiors are requested from various quarters, and the doors of the Institute open to aspirants, who keep growing ever more numerous; these, after some time of testing, if found capable, are sent wherever their work is needed. This is the reason the regular novitiate could not, in those early times, be established; this is why Sister Anna del Salvatore, who during her brief apprenticeship had given clear signs of being accomplished in every virtue and of therefore having the best dispositions for religious life, was sent elsewhere to edify by her conduct, fulfilling the mission God had assigned her.

Most scrupulous in observing the Holy Gospel Precepts and the Rules of the Institute, the good Sister soon made herself loved in the new House too, for her submissiveness, her most gentle nature, the little regard she had for herself, the severity with which she judged herself, always accusing herself of being full of faults and considering herself, in every act, in need of pity, and for the charity with which she carried out the duties entrusted to her. She was admirable at the bedside of the sick, to whom she brought consolation, peace, comfort, blessing. She was admirable when, withdrawn in the silence of the humble little Chapel, she conversed with her Jesus. Who, who could ever have followed her in the sublime impulses of her heart, passionate for her Divine Spouse? She had no other will, no other desire, than to sacrifice herself to do good to others and to give glory to God, laboring tirelessly in the field of holy Church.

The good news of the Sister's truly edifying conduct easily reached the ears of Mother Gattorno, who, needing a good and capable Superior for the founding of a new House, called Sister Anna del Salvatore to herself and, after holding a long conversation with her, in which she surely must have probed her soul, appointed her to the important and difficult office.

VI. The Superior Sister Anna del Salvatore in the Exercise of Her Duties

It is needless to say that the most obedient Sister did not show herself reluctant to accept the mandate entrusted to her; but in her great humility she pointed out to the Mother that the esteem and trust placed in her were unfounded. She was not ashamed to accuse herself of being full of faults, she laid bare even the slightest shortcomings, which in anyone less virtuous than herself would have gone unnoticed; she said that she, imperfect as she was, could never serve as a good example to the sisters entrusted to her, whom she would never know how to provide for wisely, since in her gross ignorance and inexperience she would never manage to benefit her Community, however small it might be. She begged, she implored the Mother to excuse her, for the good of the Institute, from this office, declaring herself ready to accept much more willingly and calmly any other task, even one of the humblest. And when she learned that the Mother was unmovable in her resolve, she submitted to the Will of God, which was made known to her through her, and set out, not without hesitation, however, for her destination.

And here begins the long series of acts of prompt and blind obedience to every order from above, of sacrifice, of self-denial, of humility, of charity, of virginal chastity, of fervor, of trust in Providence, of resignation, of penance, of diligent industry, performed by Sister Anna del Salvatore. These acts luminously attest to the high grace the Lord had granted his favorite daughter, so that she, while striving to sanctify her own soul, might serve as a sure guide to her fellow sisters on the difficult and dangerous path they would have to travel to reach the goal of their ardent desires, namely, the enjoyment of eternal Blessedness.

The early days of her superiorship were very painful for Sister Anna del Salvatore. Setting up a new House, if always a grave task in itself, becomes most difficult when the necessary means are lacking. And how many times the poor sister might have lost courage, drawn back before ever-new obstacles, and returned to lay the mandate entrusted to her at the feet of the Mother, had her unshaken faith in God's help not marvelously sustained her! In the saddest moments, when her soul was weighed down under the enormous burden of her many tedious duties and the struggles she had to bear, Sister Anna del Salvatore prostrated herself at the foot of the altar or shut herself in her little cell, and there, weeping, begged God, the Virgin Mary, St. Anne, and all the Saints of Paradise to work for her, since she felt herself powerless for everything. And comforted by prayer and by the confidence that she had not implored Heaven's help in vain, indeed already certain of having obtained it, she dried her tears, returned to her work, and, in the brief hours of respite, often taking time from sleep, wrote to her beloved Mother the most consoling and affectionate letters, in which, speaking to her only of beautiful things, never mentioning, for fear of grieving her, the anguish in which she often found herself, she commended herself to her prayers so that the Glorious Mother St. Anne might keep her present before the Lord, so that He would always watch over her and help her carry out the orders of her Superiors, which were sacred to her. Mother Gattorno answered each of her letters, encouraging her to think that God would take note of her conduct, for which one day a worthy reward would be given her, praising her for all she did and lovingly and wisely advising her to continue in doing good. And the grateful and devoted daughter kissed and re-kissed that letter as a sacred thing, laughing and weeping together for joy, and, enflamed by the sense of her own duty and by the promise of the reward she would earn by fulfilling it, found that her cross was too light compared to the happiness she would later attain by bearing it with resignation, and begged the Lord to make it heavier still, by adding other new tribulations. And these certainly were not lacking, for she met them at every turn: now she had to struggle with the Administration of the pious Shelter, which raised futile pretexts to contravene the agreed terms and thereby harm the Institute to which she belonged; now she had to overcome the reluctance of the residents to submit to the will of those caring for them; often it was the overly excitable nature of one sister that seriously worried her; then the momentary illness or sickness of another that grieved her. And if to this already heavy burden the Superior had to carry is added the insufficiency of means to provide the Community's needs, which often occurred, and the continual fear she felt of harming the Order through her own ignorance and incompetence, or of being, through her faults, a scandal to her fellow sisters, or else of not showing herself sufficiently charitable towards them, one will have an exact idea of the state of mind of Sister Anna del Salvatore. She, however, sustained by superhuman grace, never let her Superiors, nor her secular subordinates, nor even the nuns themselves, know of her sufferings; she always presented herself to everyone with a cheerful face and a serene spirit. The outpourings of her inner grief were all for Jesus, whom she had chosen as her intimate confidant. At the foot of the Cross, then, she laid down her anxieties, saying: "O my Crucified One, I suffer, it is true; but my suffering is always little compared to the very much that, with my sins, I have made and still make You suffer, infinite Goodness, worthy of being infinitely loved. Send me, send me, O Jesus, other, crueler sorrows, and I, in atonement for my unforgivable faults, will bear them, ever blessing your holy Will." Sister Anna del Salvatore accused herself before God as guilty, she who knew no guilt, for in her lay the whole of Christian perfection.

I wish I could adequately show here the holy joy with which she put into practice every precept of the holy Rules; the affectionate solicitude with which she watched at the bedside of the sick, into whose souls, with the sweet serenity of her spirit, she knew how to instill courage, hope, and resignation. I wish I could adequately show to what degree the sense of her own nothingness reached in her, and the painful shame she felt on hearing others weave her praises, against which she protested with all possible energy, heaping upon herself the most humbling epithets. I would be glad to make known to whoever reads me how merciful, indulgent, compassionate, loving Sister Anna del Salvatore was towards anyone at all, while being without mercy, indulgence, compassion, or love for herself, to the point of wearing down her body with the most frequent fasts, nourishing herself almost exclusively on vegetables and greens, with almost unceasing vigils, and subjecting her frail body to the most tormenting disciplines. I would like, I add, to be able to adequately praise all her other virtues, brought to the degree of perfection, which her spirit held within itself, but however hard I tried, I could never do more than set before the eyes a very faint reflection of the dazzling colors that radiate from this precious gem of holy Church. Her holiness, her works, and her merits will live through the centuries, and her name will be, wherever faith in the Religion of Christ takes root, honored, invoked, and blessed.

VII. Sister Anna del Salvatore Receives an Order from the Mother to Go to Another Posting. The Town's Discontent, Which in Vain Begs That the Order Be Revoked. The Superior's Work in the New House

Sister Anna del Salvatore's virtues, her activity, the zeal she brought to carrying out the duties of her office as Superior, had won her the esteem and trust of the Administrators of the Pious Shelter entrusted to her, who, recognizing that to her alone belonged the credit for its prosperity, now held her in great regard, and no longer opposed her just wishes. The good Superior used this influence over the Administration's mind to improve the conditions of the House and of those sheltered there, who attributed to her alone that little well-being that in so much unhappiness was granted them to enjoy. How many blessings they called down from Heaven upon the head of that angel who, under the garb of a Daughter of St. Anne, poured upon their physical and moral sufferings the most effective balms! And these invocations found a most sweet echo in the hearts of the Sisters, who felt for their Superior, who had a heart of such great charity for them as to sacrifice herself entirely to lighten their toil even a little, a boundless affection.

One cannot easily imagine, then, how painful it was when, in that House, the unexpected announcement came that the Superior was, by order of the Mother, to go to another posting, where her active and intelligent work was needed to set things in order. And while Sister Anna del Salvatore, without losing time and full of trust in her beloved Mother, prepared to obey, the Administration, the sheltered residents, and the better part of the town sent entreaties to the Mother, asking her to be so good as to revoke the order given to the Superior, who, as they asserted in their petitions, was the blessing of that House and of the town.

The Reverend Mother answered everyone, showing herself grateful for the proof of affectionate esteem shown to a Daughter of St. Anne, and consequently to the whole Institute, while at the same time regretting that she could not comply with the expressed wish, because the good of the Institute itself required the order to be carried out promptly. And the Superior departed, leaving there the most grateful memory of herself, and, accompanied by the good wishes everyone made for her, set out for her new posting.

Having arrived there, she found herself facing difficulties that at first seemed insurmountable to her. A weak spirit would have been intimidated, thinking of the new hardships awaiting it, and would have declined the office, all the more since at that moment the devil did not fail to work, exaggerating the bleakness of her position, to induce the Superior to turn aside from the straight path upon which she had set herself and was progressing by great strides. But Sister Anna del Salvatore joined, to her boundless trust in God's help, strength of spirit and an iron will in attaining the good, and so, calm and resigned, she turned her thoughts to the Institute, to which she was most happy to belong, and to her dear Mother, to whom she sought to give every possible consolation, and declared herself ready to sustain the struggle, so long as she did something that would benefit the one and please the other.

She found herself in a very poor House, therefore lacking everything, which took in poor and endangered girls, who were supported partly by very slight fees and partly by Providence. And so the good Superior, always by force of that spirit of sublime charity that led her to sacrifice herself for the good of others, knocked tirelessly at the doors of the wealthy to obtain from them the help without which her poor little daughters (so she called those taken in) would have died of hunger. The thought of a humiliating refusal did not turn her from her painful daily pilgrimage; Jesus had suffered something far more humiliating, painful, and ignominious out of love for mankind, and comforted by this thought she would leave the mansion where the offering had been refused her, without rancor, rather with a cheerful and serene spirit, and would present herself at another house, trusting in better success. And when, in the evening, tired from the long walking, worn down by hardship, exhausted from weakness for not having touched food all day, weighed down by the anxieties she had suffered, she returned home, and, having calculated the offerings received, found herself able to provide for the next day's needs, with what gratitude she raised her mind to the Lord, who had granted her that grace, and with what fervor she prayed and had others pray for the benefactors! She forgot all her sufferings, and, gathering the Sisters and young women around her, would spend time speaking with them of the infinite Goodness and Mercy of God, who never denies his help to one who places their trust in Him, and she invited them always to hope in Heaven.

But the thought of having to provide, with no means or with very scant and uncertain means, for the Community's daily needs was for her of slight importance compared to the care she took for the religious and moral education of the young women entrusted to the Sisters. She knew very well that those unfortunate girls came for the most part from families where religious and moral feeling certainly did not reach the degree that would have been necessary for them, born and raised in such surroundings, to later know how to guard themselves against evil; and so the Superior directed all her care to making of them model young women, who would then become women of tried and tested virtue.

How prompt and energetic she was in correcting their faults, and how happy she was when she saw her work come to a good end! She felt at ease in the midst of those young women, whom she loved with a mother's love, and would have made any sacrifice to spare them sorrow and hardship. And they held her as a mother, asked her for advice, listened to her corrections, and sought to grow up good in order to satisfy her wishes.

Her mission, however, did not end here: after having provided for the House, she, aided by the spontaneous and generous labor of the sisters who, inspired by her virtues, tried to model themselves on her, poured out the treasures of her confined charity at the bedside of those poor sick who, unable for special reasons to be admitted to the Hospital, were cared for by the Daughters of St. Anne free of charge at home.

A life of unspeakable hardship and toil is that of the nursing sister, especially when she must attend to the sick who swim in the most appalling misery. These unfortunates need light and nourishing food, and often lack even a crust of black bread; they need cleanliness of their person and of the bed on which they lie, and it is not rare for them to be wrapped in a shirt in tatters, so filthy as to cause disgust, lying on a foul straw pallet, without sheets, and covered with rags that, when they were well, had served as their clothing. In the midst of this sea of filth and misery, the nursing Daughters of St. Anne live continually, having, as has already been said, the fulfillment of this mission as their chief purpose.

Let it not be thought, however, that the nurse's life, most burdensome for anyone, was so for Sister Anna del Salvatore too; no, she found in the exercise of this task of hers such delight as she had never felt its equal, and often said she was grateful to God for having destined her to it, and for having thus procured for her the undeserved favor of doing something pleasing to Jesus by serving, as much as she could, the poor sick.

It is needless, then, to say how, moved by these feelings, she was always the first to hasten where the toil was heaviest, the treatment most tedious and repugnant, the danger most likely. And while she required the sisters to have sufficient rest to recover the strength lost in vigils and exertions, while she required every possible precaution to be taken to guard against contagious illnesses, she herself, always on her feet, always ready, with no care for her own life, stood day and night at the bedside of the languishing, and with her angelic smile, with her words full of charity, relieved the sick and comforted them to hope and resignation. And when, in the morning, after having spent an exhausting night, she returned to the House, to the sisters who bustled around her urging her to rest, she, always smiling and affectionate, thanking them, answered that she was not the least bit tired, and withdrew to the Chapel to await the moment of nourishing herself on the flesh of her Jesus, whence she would draw the strength for her life, which the continual fasts and vigils were consuming.

Dear and holy creature, who did not act out of love of vainglory but only out of the sublime feeling of the most disinterested charity, did you hope your virtue would remain hidden? Did you hope to pass through the world unnoticed?

When winter slowly dies into spring, to greet the season in which nature awakens to new life, the first to spring up is the violet, a gentle flower, image of modesty. It grows among the grass, making no show of itself, a small, pale, utterly simple wildflower, almost seeking to hide itself from every gaze, so that no one may find it. And yet its sweet scent betrays it, and everyone admires it and praises its beauty and its usefulness.

Like the humble violet, good Sister Anna del Salvatore, working in silence, wrapped in modest mystery, spread around her the pleasing fragrance of her virtues, which, however, did not long remain hidden. And it was not long before, passing blessed from mouth to mouth out of the hovels, her name made its way into the mansions, and everyone, poor and rich alike, enthused by the wonders of such charity and self-denial, began to extol to the skies that lofty creature sent by God to earth as a comfort for human miseries.

It is no wonder, then, that Sister Anna del Salvatore had soon become the town's favorite, and so great was the esteem and respect she had won that she was often asked for advice and comfort, not only material but also spiritual. And she, in her incomparable goodness, satisfied, as best she could, others' wishes, not, however, without first excusing herself by heaping upon herself the most humbling epithets of folly and incompetence.

From the regard in which the Superior was held sprang great good for the House. On her rounds for alms, no one dared any longer to refuse his offering to one who, together with her fellow sisters, was so generous in charity towards others. Everyone thought it right and dutiful not to refuse charity to those who bore hardships of every kind in order to do good, and if the Community had before often lacked what it needed, afterwards it had enough to meet every need, and not only that, but enough to furnish the House modestly as well. And all this prosperity thanks to that aura of devoted affection surrounding the Superior, to whom one no longer knew how to refuse anything. And so, while the poor, unable to do anything else for the good Daughters of St. Anne, prayed for them and blessed them, the rich were towards them lavish with every consideration, counting it a true honor to be able to guess the Superior's wishes in order to fulfill them.

To increase the favorable opinion most people had formed of Sister Anna del Salvatore, an event occurred that deserves to be noted. There was in the boarding school a young woman whose fees were paid by a pious person who took care of her. One day it was suddenly announced to the poor girl that the person by whom she was so generously supported had died; and misfortune would have it that the unhappy girl could not even have the comfort of the Superior's motherly words, because she was confined to bed, gravely ill.

Oppressed by the painful thought of finding herself now alone in the world, the poor girl reasoned no more, and at night, in the height of her distress, put matches in a glass of water and swallowed the poisonous drink in one gulp. One can imagine the Sisters' fright when, hearing the cries of the poisoned girl, they rushed to her and learned of the dreadful event. The Superior was at once informed, who, though burning with the most violent fever, leapt from her bed, ran to the poor girl, and, seeing her with the marks of death on her face, threw herself on her knees with arms outstretched in the form of a cross and offered a fervent prayer to the Crucified One.

Meanwhile the doctor and the priest were sent for, but when they arrived the young woman no longer needed them, having miraculously expelled all the poison. At this sudden recovery the sisters exclaimed at the Superior's miracle, the priest and the doctor looked at one another, astonished at what they saw, and in whoever learned of the event there arose a boundless trust in her who, through her prayers and her trust in God, had saved a creature from a death as desperate as that of one who takes her own life.

Because of the esteem, then, that the Superior deservedly enjoyed, and consequently the whole Community, relations between the entire citizenry and the Daughters of St. Anne were of the best, and there was general regret when it became known that the Mother, having in her wisdom thought it necessary to assign the Superior another duty, was withdrawing her from that House. How many tokens of affection she received! And with what humility she kept repeating to those who told her it would not be possible to replace her adequately, that she was the least of the Daughters of St. Anne, and that any of them who went to replace her would certainly do better than she! O holy virtue of Humility, how you magnify before God the souls in whom you dwell!

Having installed the new Superior, having implored God's help upon her fellow sisters, desolate at her departure, and blessed the young women sobbing sorrowfully at the loss of their affectionate Mother, having charged the benefactors not to abandon the House, Sister Anna del Salvatore, as always, obeyed the orders she received and, moved, left the place where, if she had suffered, she had also had many consolations, practicing in every way the lofty virtue of Charity.

notes.orsipos-en-fn437: The "benefactress" to whom she wrote the following day, April 9, is Princess Emilia di Fitalia. She announced to her a "scourge" threatening Sicily; a month later, in two letters, she specified that for the city of Palermo the scourge would be cholera. On June 11, moreover, she informed her that the prophecy of the earthquake had come true, since, according to news received the day before, June 10, strong tremors had shaken the whole region of Etna. Again, in a letter of June 26 to the same princess, she assured her that, according to an answer from Sister Anna del Salvatore, the city of Palermo would not be affected by the cholera epidemic.
notes.orsipos-en-fn438: Emilia Laberiska, born on June 21, 1847 in the Governorate of Warsaw, in Ohexie, married the Prince of Fitalia, Gerolamo Settimo, of Palermo.
notes.orsipos-en-fn440: Cardinal Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, born in Naples on April 10, 1885, was ordained a priest in 1879, appointed bishop and apostolic nuncio to Brussels in 1899, and created a cardinal in 1911. He died in Rome on February 16, 1948.
